FoveaNav

Learning Task-Relevant Gaze
for Robust Visual Navigation

A gaze policy trained with reinforcement learning selects where to focus in the camera image. A navigation model trained from expert demonstrations uses gaze to reweight attention over full-image features and predict the robot’s path.

Paper (PDF) Video 3 min How it works

850 real-robot trials across five tasks. 425 trials per method. See the results.

Real-robot results

We test whether the robot completes each task when the scene differs from training. These out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions include distractors, new obstacles, and changed signs or backgrounds. FoveaNav achieves 90–100% success across the four tasks below; BC achieves 0–38%.

How FoveaNav works

At inference, gaze selects a location in the camera image. A Gaussian map reweights the navigation transformer’s cross-attention to emphasize features near that point, while features from the rest of the image remain available.

  1. Select a gaze location

    A learned policy chooses a point in the image using visual features and recent gaze history.

  2. Reweight visual attention

    A Gaussian map emphasizes features near that point in the navigation transformer’s cross-attention. The full image remains available.

  3. Predict the robot’s path

    The navigation transformer uses the reweighted cross-attention to predict a future trajectory.

How the components are trained

ComponentRoleTraining
Gaze policySelect a gaze locationPPO using trajectory prediction error on recorded expert trajectories
Navigation modelPredict a trajectory using gaze-weighted cross-attentionBehavior cloning from expert demonstrations

Training begins with full-image behavior cloning, then alternates PPO updates to the gaze policy with behavior-cloning updates to the navigation model. No human gaze annotations are used. Each task uses a separately trained model.

Full-image gaze weighting vs. a crop

For red-bag following with obstacles, we compare Gaussian weighting over the full image with a gaze-centered crop. Both variants use an RL-trained gaze policy.

Successful trials out of 10 attempts per variant (paper Table II). This is a separate ablation experiment.

RL + Gaussian gaze 10 / 10
RL + hard crop 1 / 10

What happens when noise hides the target?

When image noise leaves the red bag visible, FoveaNav predicts the trajectory more accurately than BC. When noise also covers the bag, the difference between the methods becomes smaller.

This test evaluates predictions on recorded images. Lower loss means a more accurate trajectory. The 71% label measures how much the difference in loss between the two methods shrinks.
